title: Opponent Angle Rapid Playbook (draft)
content:
Slide 1 — Deck title: Opponent Angle Rapid Playbook (draft)
Speaker note: Quick field-ready deck for SEs and sellers to run a 10–20m probe against competitor narratives. Emphasis: practical redlines + one-click pilot asks.

Slide 2 — Why this deck exists
- Problem: Deals stall on abstract objections (cost, SLA, on-prem control).
- Goal: Give a compact, repeatable set of narratives and checklists to accelerate pilots and disarm competitive talking points.
- Outcome: Faster qualification -> cleared pilots -> measurable POC criteria.

Slide 3 — Audience & use cases
- Primary: Sales Engineers, Field Sellers, Solution Architects.
- Use cases: discovery calls, 1:1 SE deep dives, pilot kickoff, rapid rebuttal during demos.

Slide 4 — High-level thesis for sellers
- Lead with operational guarantees (latency, throughput, SLOs) not feature parity.
- Translate performance into customer outcomes: response time -> UX conversions, cost -> cost per session -> margin.
- Offer literal escape hatches (fallback model variants, reserved capacity) to reduce buyer risk.

Slide 5 — Competitive snapshot (short-form)
- Competitor A: Large cloud AI provider
  - Strengths: scale, single-pane billing, marketplace reach.
  - Weaknesses: black-box performance profiles, limited model variants for aggressive fallbacks, unpredictable unit economics at low utilization.
- Competitor B: Pure self-host runtime/vendor
  - Strengths: control, deep HW customization.
  - Weaknesses: heavy ops, slow upgrades, inconsistent observability across teams.
- Competitor C: Open-source model tools/DIY
  - Strengths: cost upside at scale, flexibility.
  - Weaknesses: integration time, no SLA, missing guardrails for canary rollouts.

Slide 6 — Battlecard format (how to use)
- Frame the objection -> Quick fact -> Rebuttal script -> Proof point / Ask.
- Keep rebuttals <30s. If it's a deep technical objection, move to SE deep dive and book follow-up.

Slide 7 — Example battlecard: "They're cheaper (we can self-host)"
- Quick fact: Self-hosting has lower sticker compute sometimes but high ops lead time (weeks-months) and ongoing engineering maintenance.
- Rebuttal script: "Totally—self-hosting can be cost-effective at steady-state, but the hidden costs are ramp, reliability, and unpredictable throughput during peak sessions. With Redwood, you get predictable unit economics and continuos batching/kv-caching that often beats naive self-host margins for interactive apps."
- Proof point: Pilot template with measured token/unit cost baseline + standard caching config; typical customer sees 15–40% lower per-interaction cost after Optimize recommendations.
- Ask: "Can we run a 2-week controlled pilot where we run identical traffic and report on cost/latency delta? We’ll provide dashboard access and a short teardown doc."

Slide 8 — Example battlecard: "We need on-prem/airgap (security)"
- Quick fact: Private deployments are real but the critical tradeoffs are control vs. upgrade velocity and observability.
- Rebuttal script: "We offer Redwood Private with a customer-managed control plane and KMS/HSM integrations; many regulated customers start on Dedicated then migrate to Private for data isolation while retaining rollout policies."
- Proof point: Two-week stubbed deployment checklist + compliance artifacts (SOC2 template, audit log sample).
- Ask: "Do you have an internal security gate we can pass? If so, share one key requirement and we’ll produce a focused artifact in 48 hours."

Slide 9 — Example battlecard: "They offer better SLAs / uptime"
- Quick fact: Public cloud providers tout large network SLAs but application-level inference SLOs need architecture and fallback guarantees.
- Rebuttal script: "We pair dedicated capacity with canary rollouts, fallback to compatible model variants, and automatic region failover to meet app-level SLOs. We instrument token-level tracing so you can map incidents to code paths."
- Proof point: Incident runbook snippet and latency distribution dashboard exported from Console.
- Ask: "Can you share target P50/P95 for your key flows? We’ll map an example config and run a simulated load test."

Slide 10 — 60s pitch (what to say when buyer names a competitor)
- Acknowledge: "That’s a reasonable option — many teams start there."
- Differentiate in outcomes: "With Redwood, you’re buying production predictability: latency, unit cost, and operational controls that directly impact product metrics."
- Close for action: "Let’s lock a short pilot with three concrete success metrics — we’ll own the instrumentation so you can compare apples-to-apples."

Slide 11 — Quick technical redlines (for SEs)
- Memory/kv cache pattern: ask for median sequence lengths, batching patterns, and peak concurrent requests.
- Model compatibility: verify whether customer's model needs KV cache warm-up or supports quantized variants.
- Network topology: request topology diagram for VPC/private link if doing Private pilot.
- Logging/audit: which event types (inference request, model switch, fallback) are required?

Slide 12 — Pilot template (2-week lightweight)
- Week 0: Scope alignment + traffic replay sample + measurement hooks (tracing + token cost).
- Week 1: Baseline run on buyer infra (if self-hosting) or baseline run on Redwood hosted.
- Week 2: Apply Optimize recommendations (batching, caching, quantization) -> compare.
- Success metrics (pick 2–3): P95 latency delta, cost per 1k tokens, error rate during peak.

Slide 13 — Objection scripts cheat-sheet (quick bullets)
- "We can build this ourselves" -> "How long do you estimate to reach feature parity plus operational telemetry? If <4 weeks, let’s talk a ramp plan; if >4 weeks, a pilot will de-risk the decision."
- "Vendor lock-in" -> "We support pinned model versions and exportable configs for migration; rollbacks are one-click."
- "Cost is unclear" -> "We’ll provide tokenized cost reports and a modeled projection for 6 months at your expected utilization."

Slide 14 — Field play examples (short anecdotes)
- Fintech customer: avoided 2-week outage by switching to a reserved capacity fallback during batch job spikes.
- Marketplace: reduced per-session inference cost by 27% after applying dynamic batching + prefix caching.
- Enterprise: completed SOC2 gap analysis and migrated to Private with zero data exfiltration issues.

Slide 15 — Quick reference scripts for demos (30–60s lines)
- Latency demo opener: "Here’s how latency shapes user experience — every 300ms added latency reduces conversion by X% in similar apps. We keep that under control with dedicated pools and smart routing."
- Cost demo opener: "We surface token-level unit economics so you can see cost drivers (prompt size, model variant, batching)."

Slide 16 — Pilot ask templates (email + slack)
- Email subject: "Two-week comparison pilot with instrumentation — quick ask"
- Body bullets: 1) sample traffic + duration, 2) three success metrics, 3) minimal network access, 4) acceptance criteria and handover date.

Slide 17 — Next steps & enablement assets
- Immediate: SE to send pilot ask template; schedule 30m technical kickoff.
- Assets to attach: pilot checklist, tracing schema, SOC2 summary, cost baseline workbook.
- Success: convert pilot into reserved capacity proposal or dedicated migration plan.

Slide 18 — Appendix A: Short troubleshooting crib notes
- If P95 spikes: check batch sizing, KV hit rate, and model warm-up.
- If cost is high: verify batching window, prefix length, and unnecessary top-k sampling parameters.
- If fallbacks trigger: confirm model compatibility matrix and rollback window.

Slide 19 — Appendix B: Example outputs we can hand over
- One-page pilot teardown (CSV of metrics), latency heatmap PNG, cost-by-route table.

Slide 20 — Appendix C: Links & artifacts
- Pilot workbook (sheet link placeholder), runbook PR, customer-facing case study stub.

Speaker closing note: This is intentionally compact — the goal is repeatability. Field teams should adapt one or two battlecards per call rather than recite the whole deck. Keep this as a living doc (tag updates to JIRA-GTM-872).

End of deck — workspace notes: still draft. Action owners: Riley (owner) to run SE dry-run on 11/24; Anika to draft pilot workbook; Mohammed to produce SOC2 Q&A snippet.
